summary:
Liguori traces the evolution from inline completion to chat, vibe coding, and frontier development. She personally felt only 10-20% gains across earlier phases but observes Amazon pilots achieving a median 4.5x and sometimes over 10x productivity improvement. Frontier developers are defined by three behaviors: writing only 1-2% of code, running agents for hours without intervention, and minimizing idle time by running multiple agents in parallel.

Two early pathfinder cases are presented. The Bedrock Mantle team built a new inference data plane in 76 days with six people versus an estimate of 30 over 18 months, but the team included two distinguished engineers with deep LLM and distributed systems expertise. A Prime Video 10-day sprint with six engineers cut a 90-week estimate to 24 weeks, but the engineers had no on-call duties, limited meetings, and three weeks of pre-scoped tasks. Neither was reproducible on ordinary teams.

Amazon Stores then studied 50 normal teams on existing brownfield codebases for most of a year. Ninety percent used Kiro alongside internal tools. Half achieved under 3x deployment velocity; the other half hit a median 4.5x and sometimes above 10x. The tool was not the variable; teams that intentionally changed their way of working pulled ahead.

Five day-to-day habits emerged: invest in agent context and prune it as models improve; slow down to speed up by doing real work in brownfield codebases (error messages, MCP servers, restructuring, even language changes); feed agents with self-validation criteria instead of babysitting 30-60 second loops; make intent explicit in spec documents before arguing with generated code; and shift testing left with deterministic local mocks so agents can self-correct in fast feedback loops, with linters, unit, integration, performance, and security tests.

Liguori warns that adoption is not nirvana. Engineers risk 'flow mat' burnout, staying up late to perfect overnight prompts. Cognitive load rises from shifting between parallel terminal tabs. Reviewing AI output is harder than writing it for early-career engineers who lack reviewing muscle. Organizations must accept slowing down to speed up and resist viral pressure to ship 20 PRs a day. Rolling frontier development out too broadly too fast forfeits learnings; Amazon is now scaling from 50 to roughly 2,000 teams in 2026. Finally, code-writing is no longer the bottleneck. When products can be built in one to two months, decision-making and launch review become the long pole. Frontier engineering teams now spend more time deciding than coding, so fast, easily reversible decisions matter most.

sections.title: Evolution into frontier development
sections.summary: Liguori introduces herself as a senior principal engineer at AWS working on Kiro and walks through the evolution from inline completion to chat, vibe coding, and frontier development. She notes only 10-20% personal gains across earlier phases, while Amazon pilots show a median 4.5x and sometimes above 10x. Frontier development is defined by three behaviors: 1-2% hand-written code, agents running for hours, and minimizing idle time via parallel agents.

sections.title: Pathfinder case: Bedrock Mantle in 76 days
sections.summary: Bedrock Mantle built a new inference data plane in 76 days with six people versus an estimate of 30 over 18 months. The team included two distinguished engineers with deep LLM and distributed systems expertise, making the result impressive but hard to reproduce.

sections.title: Pathfinder case: Prime Video 10-day sprint
sections.summary: A Prime Video 10-day sprint with six engineers cut a 90-week project estimate to 24 weeks. However, the engineers had no on-call duties, limited meetings, and three weeks of pre-scoped tasks, so the result was again not representative of normal engineering life.

sections.title: Amazon Stores pilot: 50 normal teams
sections.summary: Amazon Stores watched 50 teams with a normal seniority mix on existing brownfield codebases for most of a year, using deployment velocity to production as the metric. Ninety percent used Kiro alongside internal tools. Half achieved under 3x; the other half hit a median 4.5x and sometimes above 10x. The tool was not the variable; teams that intentionally changed their way of working pulled ahead.

sections.title: Habits 1-4: context, slow-down, feeding, intent
sections.summary: The five habits are day-to-day practices, not one-off sprints. Habit 1: invest in agent context by writing tacit knowledge into steering and skills files, then pruning as models improve so obsolete workarounds do not bloat context. Habit 2: slow down to speed up; productivity often drops first because brownfield codebases need error message fixes, new tools/MCP servers, restructuring, or even language changes like TypeScript or Rust for better compiler feedback. Habit 3: feed agents rather than babysit them, enabling self-validation against quality bars instead of 30-60 second loops. Habit 4: make intent explicit through behavior-driven specs before arguing with generated code.

sections.title: Habits 4-5: spec intent and shift-left testing
sections.summary: Liguori elaborates on Habits 4 and 5. Spec-first iteration in a document is easier than arguing over code changes scattered across a codebase. Habit 5 is shift-left testing: linters, unit, integration, performance, and security tests give the agent a fast feedback loop for self-correction. Teams mock services locally with deterministic responses so the agent can run entirely on the laptop without spinning up cloud services, multiplying the agent's correction loops and productivity.

sections.title: Burnout, FOMO, and cognitive load
sections.summary: Adopting these habits is not nirvana. Liguori flags burnout risks, including 'flow mat' where engineers stay up late to perfect overnight prompts. Cognitive load rises from shifting between parallel terminal tabs. Reviewing AI output is often harder than writing it, especially for early-career engineers who lack reviewing muscle, unlike senior engineers who have spent years reviewing others' code.

sections.title: What organizations have to change
sections.summary: Organizations must accept slowing down to speed up. Leaders must stop demanding immediate velocity gains because teams need two months to invest in the codebase, best practices, and hard habit changes. Resisting viral pressure to ship 20 PRs a day is critical. Rolling frontier development out too broadly too fast forfeits learnings; Amazon's 2026 plan is to scale from 50 teams to roughly 2,000 teams gradually so each organization can develop its own best practices and context.

sections.title: Decision speed becomes the bottleneck
sections.summary: Code-writing is no longer the bottleneck. With products buildable in one to two months, decision-making and launch review become the long pole. When a product took 9-12 months to build, two-month decision and approval phases did not matter; now they do. Frontier engineering teams spend more time deciding than coding, so fast, easily reversed decisions matter most. Liguori closes with the takeaway that frontier engineering is about intentionally changing how you work, forming new habits across teams and organizations, and freeing yourself from being in the loop.

evidence.excerpt: completely anecdotally, based on my own experience, I've really only felt maybe 10 to 20% more productive with all of these phases that have come before. But now inside of Amazon, we've been running pilots with different teams across the company and we've been seeing a median of 4.5x productivity improvement and sometimes more than 10x.
evidence.supports: Pilot teams achieved a median 4.5x and sometimes more than 10x productivity improvement, far above the 10-20% personal gain Liguori felt earlier.

evidence.excerpt: Frontier developers write maybe 1 to 2% of the code that they produce. The rest is agents. The second is that they interact with their agents infrequently. They'll aim to get their coding assistant to run for up to hours at a time without their intervention. And third is that they minimize idle time. These frontier developers tend to run multiple agents in parallel
evidence.supports: Frontier development is defined by hands-off coding, long unattended runs, and parallel agent execution.

evidence.excerpt: They saw that for half of the teams, they achieved less than 3x increase. And what they found that was the difference between seeing less than 3x productivity increase, these teams that saw a median of 4.5x, and and in some cases more than 10, was how they used the tools.
evidence.supports: Among 50 normal teams, half were under 3x and the other half hit a median 4.5x with peaks above 10x.

evidence.excerpt: 90% of these teams used Kiro, among other internal tools that we have, and what they found was it wasn't about the tools, it was about the way that they worked. The teams that achieved step function improvements intentionally changed the way that they worked
evidence.supports: The tool was not the deciding factor; intentionally changing how the team worked was.

evidence.excerpt: it's a lot easier to to iterate with the model in kind of a back and forth conversation about a document than it is about code that's code changes that are spread across a code base.
evidence.supports: Iterating intent in a spec document is easier than arguing about scattered code changes.

evidence.excerpt: give the agent that fast feedback loop. Because that's what lets it go off for hours at a time and self-correct. The agent is going to make mistakes and that's fine. But if you give it the right signals, it can self-correct
evidence.supports: Habit 5 is shift-left testing with a fast feedback loop so agents can self-correct over long runs.

evidence.excerpt: I've seen teams adding linters, adding unit tests, integration tests, performance tests, security tests. These are all things we all know we should have been doing all along. This is good engineering hygiene and practices. But now the ROI is, I think, finally high enough
evidence.supports: Shift-left testing brings long-known hygiene practices (linters, unit/integration/performance/security tests) into agent-driven workflows where the ROI is finally justified.

evidence.excerpt: mock out services... mock services that run entirely locally with deterministic responses because it lets the agent do everything locally... the more that your agent can get fast feedback means the more loops that it can can do
evidence.supports: Local deterministic mocks let agents run entirely on the laptop for faster feedback loops and more self-corrections.

evidence.excerpt: flow mat is real. We've been seeing engineers staying up late late at night trying to get that perfect prompt that's going to make their agent run for hours overnight
evidence.supports: Engineers risk 'flow mat' burnout from trying to perfect overnight prompts.

evidence.excerpt: The cognitive load increases as you run these multiple agents in parallel. You're constantly shifting between terminal tabs.
evidence.supports: Running multiple agents in parallel raises cognitive load from shifting between terminal tabs.

evidence.excerpt: reviewing AI output is often harder for some than than actually writing it, especially early in career. Senior engineers have have already spent a large portion of their career reviewing others code. But early career engineers don't have that muscle yet
evidence.supports: Reviewing AI output is harder than writing it for early-career engineers who lack reviewing muscle.

evidence.excerpt: Why are you not going faster? Um and that's because you have to take those two months to invest in your code base, to figure out the best practices for your team, to make hard habit changes on your team.
evidence.supports: Leaders must accept slowing down to speed up; teams need two months of investment before velocity rises.
